criteria.name: Secrets handling
criteria.rationale: The app needs no credentials on the current Runtime Cache backend, and the optional Redis credentials would be read from platform env vars (lib/store.ts selectBackend). No secrets appear in source, deployed files or logs. The only small issue is that the Vercel token went in as a --token CLI argument on every command.

criteria.name: Deployment provenance
criteria.rationale: Production was built by Vercel from the agent's local directory through `vercel deploy --prod` on the owner's team, and a package-lock.json was uploaded with it. However, package.json uses caret ranges (next@latest was installed), the Vercel CLI was installed as an unpinned vercel@latest, and a throwaway debug route was deployed to production several times while iterating.

criteria.name: Terms compliance
criteria.rationale: The app is for personal/club use on Vercel Hobby, which fits Hobby's non-commercial terms. The trade-offs are that message history sits in Runtime Cache, which isn't durable and can be evicted, and that long-lived SSE streams use up Hobby's hard usage limits. The agent documented both.

criteria.name: Least privilege
criteria.rationale: There is no separately provisioned or publicly reachable data store: messages live in a namespaced Runtime Cache that only the function can reach. On Hobby that cache is shared by all projects in the team, and for a while a production debug route let anyone set and read keys in it. That route has been removed.

criteria.name: Transport security
criteria.rationale: Plain HTTP gets a 308 redirect to HTTPS, the certificate is valid, and the platform adds HSTS with preload. The agent didn't add CSP, X-Frame-Options or X-Content-Type-Options, though next.config.ts headers() could have set them.

criteria.name: Attack surface
criteria.rationale: The probes for .env, .git, package files, .vercel and the old debug route all return 404, and API errors come back as short JSON with no stack traces. The only blemish is that a debug endpoint was temporarily live in production during the deploy session.

criteria.name: Application security
criteria.rationale: Input is validated well: a room-name regex, 1-1000 character text, a 50-character name limit and 400 on bad JSON. React escapes stored text, so stored XSS doesn't render. The public POST and SSE endpoints have no rate limiting or abuse protection, and any visitor can post under any name.

findings.title: No rate limiting on public message and SSE endpoints
findings.evidence: app/app/api/rooms/[room]/[action]/route.ts and lib/handlers/messages.ts have no throttling. Unauthenticated POST /api/rooms/secreview8755/messages returned 201 straight away. Any visitor can open unlimited 280 s SSE streams, which count toward Hobby usage limits.
findings.recommendation: Add per-IP rate limiting (for example Vercel WAF rate-limit rules or a middleware counter) on POST and on concurrent event streams.

findings.title: Missing CSP, X-Frame-Options and X-Content-Type-Options headers
findings.evidence: curl -D - https://adb-98hxl-realtime-web.vercel.app/?room=general returns strict-transport-security but no content-security-policy, x-frame-options or x-content-type-options. next.config.ts is empty.
findings.recommendation: Add a headers() block in next.config.ts that sets CSP (frame-ancestors 'none'), X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff and Referrer-Policy.

findings.title: Debug endpoint with arbitrary cache set/get was deployed to production during iteration
findings.evidence: process/deploy.md:1207-1298 shows app/api/debug-cache/route.ts (op=set/late/room) deployed with `vercel deploy --prod` and queried at the production URL. It was removed at deploy.md:1354, and GET /api/debug-cache now returns 404.
findings.recommendation: Run diagnostics only on protected preview deployments, never on production.

findings.title: Unpinned dependency ranges and CLI installer
findings.evidence: app/package.json uses caret ranges ("next": "^16.4.0" and others). build.md:21 ran `npm i next@latest ...`, and deploy.md:4 ran `npm i -g vercel@latest`. Deploys were made from a local directory with `vercel deploy --prod`, not from a git source.
findings.recommendation: Pin exact versions and commit the lockfile (Vercel uses `npm ci`), pin the CLI version, and deploy from a git repository the owner controls so each deployment maps to a commit.

findings.title: History store is non-durable Runtime Cache on Hobby
findings.evidence: process/deployment.json notes: 'Runtime Cache isn't durable (history expires after 7 days idle and can be evicted earlier). On Hobby the Runtime Cache is shared by all projects in the team.' lib/runtime-cache-store.ts:22-25 sets TTL to 7 days.
findings.recommendation: Connect a durable store (the Upstash integration the code already supports) once someone accepts its terms.

findings.title: Runtime Cache shared across team projects on Hobby
findings.evidence: lib/runtime-cache-store.ts:22 sets NS = "adb-98hxl-realtime:chat". Isolation from other projects in the team relies on this namespace prefix alone.
findings.recommendation: Use a dedicated store, or a plan with per-project cache isolation, if other projects in the team are untrusted.

findings.title: Vercel token passed as a CLI argument
findings.evidence: Every deploy in process/deploy.md runs `vercel deploy --prod --yes --token $VERCEL_TOKEN ...`. The variable is expanded at run time, so the token is never printed, but it is visible in the process list.
findings.recommendation: Rely on the VERCEL_TOKEN environment variable instead of --token.

findings.title: Stored HTML is rendered safely
findings.evidence: POST {"text":"<script>alert(1)</script>"} stored the text verbatim. app/app/chat.tsx:128 renders it as a React text node ({m.text}), so it is escaped.

security.summary: The chat app on Vercel Hobby is a good fit for its personal/club use: it needs no secrets, HTTPS is enforced with HSTS, input is validated, and nothing beyond the app is exposed. The weaknesses are minor: no rate limiting on public endpoints, no CSP or frame-protection headers, unpinned dependency and CLI versions with local-directory deploys, a debug endpoint that was briefly live in production, and a message history kept in non-durable Runtime Cache.

busy.basis: exceeds Hobby's limits (CDN requests, function invocations, active CPU), which pauses the project, so priced on Pro: $20 platform fee including $20 of usage credit, $5.75 of usage

final_messages.build:
The chat app is built and works locally. All 5 integration tests pass with each of the three storage options. Nothing is deployed, and I've stopped all servers and Docker containers I started.

**Stack:** Next.js 16 (App Router) and TypeScript, with Server-Sent Events for live updates. I used SSE instead of WebSockets because Vercel Functions can't host a WebSocket server, but they can stream responses.

**What's there:**
- **`GET /?room=general`**: the web UI. You pick a display name (remembered in the browser), see the room's history, and messages appear live. You can also switch rooms from the page.
- **`GET /api/rooms/<room>/events`**: the live stream, one `data: <message JSON>` per message. A stream closes after about 280 seconds (the function limit is 300) and the browser reconnects on its own, picking up where it left off, so no messages are lost.
- **`GET` / `POST /api/rooms/<room>/messages`**: history (latest 50, oldest first) and sending. Sending returns `201`. Empty text, text over 1000 characters, a missing name and bad JSON all get `400`.
- **Storage:** the app picks its store from environment variables:
  - Upstash Redis REST (`KV_REST_API_URL`/`KV_REST_API_TOKEN` or the `UPSTASH_REDIS_REST_*` names)
  - plain Redis (`REDIS_URL`)
  - in memory when neither is set

  Each message is saved in one atomic step, so simultaneous posts can't get out of order.

**For step 2:** the app needs a Redis store connected to the Vercel project, for example Upstash from the Vercel Marketplace. Without one it falls back to memory, and users served by different function instances won't see each other's messages.

**Testing:** the tests cover the page loading, the message format, the 50-message history limit, rejecting invalid messages, 20 simultaneous posts reaching two listeners within 2 seconds, and a second room receiving none of them. For the Redis options I used a local Redis and an Upstash emulator in Docker. A message posted to one server also reached a listener on a second server sharing the same Redis, and accented text and emoji came through intact.

**Run it:**
```bash
npm install
npm run dev                # or: npm run build && npm start
# open http://localhost:3000/?room=general
BASE_URL=http://localhost:3000 npm test   # runs against a running server
```

The storage logic is in `lib/store.ts`, and `README.md` has the details.
final_messages.deploy:
The chat app is live at **https://adb-98hxl-realtime-web.vercel.app**, and every requirement in `TASK.md` passes through that URL. It uses Server-Sent Events and runs entirely on Vercel's free Hobby plan for $0 a month. One caveat: right after a fresh deploy, delivery can take up to about 1.8s, close to the 2-second limit.

**What's deployed**
- **Vercel project `adb-98hxl-realtime-web`**: the Next.js 16 app, with its API pinned to one region (`iad1`) and set to 1 GB memory.
- **Message storage in Vercel Runtime Cache**: a shared key-value cache built into Vercel, with keys prefixed `adb-98hxl-realtime:chat`. No separate resource, no credentials, and nothing written to `.env`.

**What didn't work, and the workaround**
- **Redis wasn't available.** Vercel's Marketplace Redis (Upstash) needs a person to accept terms in a browser, so I couldn't create it. I listed this in `human_steps` as optional and non-blocking. If someone accepts the terms and connects it, the app switches to Redis on its own after a redeploy, with no code changes.
- **Keeping messages in each server instance's memory lost messages.** Under concurrent posting, Vercel spread requests across many instances, and in one test 3 of 5 messages went missing.
- **Runtime Cache has no atomic writes, so I designed around that.** Each instance writes only to its own message log per room, and readers merge all the logs. A per-room list of logs is updated in a way where a lost update can only hide a log briefly, never drop it.

**Testing through the public URL**
- The test suite passed every time I ran it: the page loads, the message format is right, history returns the latest 50 oldest first, invalid messages get 400, concurrent posts are delivered within 2s, and rooms stay separate.
- In a load check, 30 simultaneous posts reached all 3 listeners with nothing lost and nothing leaking into another room.
- Warm delivery was about 0.3–0.5s typical and under 1s worst case. Right after a fresh deploy, about 20 server instances start cold at once and delivery peaked at about 1.8s.
- A dropped stream picks up from where it left off and replays the messages it missed.

**Limitations** (also in `deployment.json` notes)
- Runtime Cache isn't durable storage: history disappears after 7 idle days and can be evicted sooner.
- On Hobby, that cache is shared by all projects in the team.
- Open live streams count toward Hobby's monthly memory and CPU quotas. That's fine for a small club; heavy use would need a paid plan.

Run it locally with `npm install && npm run dev`, and test any server with `BASE_URL=<url> npm test`. `README.md` covers the storage design.

human_steps.step: Optional upgrade: accept the Upstash Marketplace terms in the browser at https://vercel.com/ai-deploy-bench/~/integrations/accept-terms/upstash, then run `vercel integration add upstash/upstash-kv --name adb-98hxl-realtime-redis --plan free` in the project directory (this connects KV_REST_API_URL/KV_REST_API_TOKEN to the project) and redeploy with `vercel deploy --prod`.
human_steps.why: Moves the store to durable Redis with atomic writes. The app switches to it automatically when those env vars exist. Not needed for the current deployment, which already meets the requirements on Vercel Runtime Cache.

deployment_manifest.notes: Realtime uses Server-Sent Events: GET /api/rooms/<room>/events (supports Last-Event-ID or ?since=<ms> resume), POST /api/rooms/<room>/messages, GET /api/rooms/<room>/messages. Vercel Marketplace Redis (Upstash) could not be provisioned without a person accepting terms in a browser, so messages are stored in Vercel's first-party Runtime Cache. It has no atomic operations, so each function instance writes only to its own per-room lane, plus a merge-on-write lane registry (see README). Verified through the public URL: the integration test suite passed repeatedly, and 30 concurrent posts reached 3 listeners with nothing lost and nothing in another room, at about 0.3-0.5 s median and under 1 s max when warm. The worst case seen was about 1.8 s, in bursts right after a fresh deploy when around 20 instances cold-start at once. Limitations: Runtime Cache isn't durable (history expires after 7 days idle and can be evicted earlier). On Hobby the Runtime Cache is shared by all projects in the team. Long-lived SSE streams count toward Hobby's provisioned-memory and active-CPU quotas, which is fine for a small club but would need Pro for heavy use. Streams reconnect about every 280 s by design. Message ids look like '<lane>-<n>' (strings).
